Rivera secures $125K in state grants for Stauffer Park rehabilitation
Rep. Nikki Rivera
October 7, 2026 | 4:58 PM
HARRISBURG, Oct. 7
– State Rep. Nikki Rivera, D-Lancaster, helped secure $125,000 in grants from the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources to rehabilitate Stauffer Park in Manheim Township.
The $125,000 grant for the Elizabeth S. Ludgate Trust for Stauffer Park will be used to renovate the internal loop trail; construct walkways and an access drive; and make ADA access, landscaping, signage and other related site improvements.
“The creation and preservation of green spaces are critical to improving the quality of life in our communities,” Rivera said. “The walkway and trail improvements at Stauffer Park will make it more accessible, improve safety, increase community access and enhance recreational opportunities.”
The funding comes from DCNR’s Environmental Stewardship Fund, which supports state parks, conservation and outdoor recreation.

Rep. Nikki Rivera
October 7, 2026 | 12:33 PM
HARRISBURG, Oct. 7 —
As electric costs and household shutoffs reached historic highs this year, PA House Democrats introduced a bold series of bills in April intended to lower costs for everyday Pennsylvanians, hold big corporations accountable and get more energy out of Pennsylvania’s existing infrastructure. On Wednesday, House members gathered again to urge action on this crisis and renew focus on their Energy Affordability bill package.
The bills in the package are:
H.B. 1834: Data Centers and Consumers (Matzie)
H.B. 2131: Promoting Fairness in PA’s Retail Electricity Market (Boyd)
H.B. 1457: Prohibiting Weather Normalization Adjustments (Probst)
H.B. 2264: Establishing a Virtual Power Plant (VPP) Program (Davidson)
H.B. 2380: Reducing utility bills by utilizing grid-scale battery storage (Rivera)
H.B. 2223: Lowering Electric Bills by Adopting Advanced Transmission Technologies (Fiedler)
H.B. 2224: Saving Taxpayers Money by Limiting Excessive Profits for Utility Monopolies (Fiedler)
House Bill 1457, introduced by state Rep. Tarah
Probst
, D-Monroe/Pike, would save consumers money by prohibiting companies from charging Weather Normalization Adjustments, which charge customers for energy they never use.
“We’re talking today about energy affordability, but how can we expect Pennsylvanians to afford their utility bills when they can be charged more for using less energy?”
Probst
said. “Weather normalization adjustments can leave families with higher-than-expected bills simply because the weather was different than anticipated or they made the responsible choice to conserve energy. I’ve heard directly from constituents in Monroe and Pike Counties who have experienced this firsthand. House Bill 1457 would put an end to this practice and make sure Pennsylvanians aren’t punished for turning down their heat, conserving energy or simply experiencing an unusually warm winter.”
State Rep. Heather
Boyd
, D-Delaware, introduced H.B. 2131 to protect ratepayers from predatory business practices by automatically returning them to their initial service contract, unless they explicitly choose a new company. Pennsylvania’s retail energy market promises low “teaser” rates, but research shows that these contracts cost ratepayers far more than default service.
“Pennsylvanians shouldn’t have to be energy experts just to make sure they’re not paying more than they should for electricity,”
Boyd
said. “I introduced H.B. 2131 because consumers deserve transparency and a real choice when their energy contract ends. Families are already struggling with rising costs. They shouldn’t be hit with an unexpected increase because they missed the fine print. House Bill 2131 is about protecting consumers and making sure Pennsylvania’s energy market works for the people who rely on it every day.”
The package also includes H.B. 2224, which passed the House unanimously in June, that would lower consumers’ bills by limiting how much excessive profit utility companies can derive from ratepayers.
“Households in Pennsylvania should pay the appropriate cost for safe and reliable utility service, and not a dollar more,” said state Rep. Elizabeth
Fiedler
, D-Phila, the sponsor of H.B. 2224. “House Bill 2224 will set a clear rule that utilities can only earn what their actual operating costs justify. This bill could save everyday people a lot of money, potentially hundreds of dollars a year. By restoring balance to the ratemaking process, we can put an end to unjustified rate hikes, protect affordability and make sure every dollar paid by ratepayers goes toward serving the public — not lining the pockets of giant corporations.”

Davidson

Rivera raises awareness of need for funding for Duchenne muscular dystrophy at Capitol
Rep. Nikki Rivera
October 6, 2026 | 4:39 PM
HARRISBURG, Oct. 6
– State Rep. Nikki Rivera held a news conference to raise awareness about Duchenne muscular dystrophy last week at the Capitol.
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a condition that causes skeletal and heart muscle weakness that quickly gets worse with time. Symptoms usually begin by age 6 and mainly affect boys. Currently, there is no cure for the disease.
“We must ensure sustained funding for research and access to care for families impacted by this terrible disease,” Rivera said. “Investments in Duchenne muscular dystrophy research will improve the lives of those affected and get us closer to a cure for this terrible disease.”
Speakers at the news conference included: Tracy Horst who spoke about the urgent need for funding for Duchenne research; and Dan Murphy, whose son has the disease, who spoke about caring for a child with the disease.
Introduced this session, H.B. 1715 would amend the Newborn Child Testing Act to include Duchenne muscular dystrophy to avert preventable complications, reduce long-term healthcare costs, and provide families with critical resources and support.

Kosierowski kratom bill unanimously passes PA House
Rep. Nikki Rivera
October 5, 2026 | 4:25 PM
HARRISBURG, Oct. 5
– Legislation that would regulate the sale of natural kratom products and prohibit the sale of synthetic kratom unanimously passed the House today, the bill’s sponsor, state Rep. Bridget Kosierowski, D-Lackawanna, announced.
Kratom is a plant from southeast Asia used for its psychoactive properties.
The Food and Drug Administration and U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
have recommended that the Drug Enforcement Agency classify 7-OH as a Schedule 1 controlled substance
– placing it in the same category as heroin and LSD.
House Bill 2657 would create a statutory framework for the sale, distribution and quality control of kratom products within Pennsylvania. Retailers registered with the state would be allowed to sell natural-leaf kratom products to people 21 and over. Packaging would have to list the manufacturer's name and address, carry a warning that the products have not been evaluated by the FDA and make no medical claims. Packaging would also have to be child resistant and designed not to appeal to minors. Kratom products would be subject to the tobacco tax.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health would enforce standards and collect taxes.
The bill would also ban the sale of synthetic or adulterated kratom products, including those that contain more than 0.5% alkaloid composition of 7-hydroxymitragynine or 7-OH, a compound found in only trace amounts in the kratom leaf. Sellers of these illegal products would be subject to criminal penalties.
Kosierowski said that this legislation was prompted by the rising number of overdoses where kratom was found, either alone or with other drugs. There have been 33 in Pennsylvania since 2025, according to the DOH.  Calls to poison control centers regarding kratom have also risen this year, with
106 from Jan. 1 through June 30, including 41 involving 7-OH
. The calls involved individuals from 12 months to 80 years of age; naloxone was administered in 25 cases, and 14 individuals required mechanical ventilation.
“What we know and don’t know about kratom are both terrifying,” Kosierowski said. “We already are aware that kratom is terribly addictive and can kill users, but what really worries me, given the drug’s soaring popularity and widespread availably, is that there is limited research on the long-term effects of taking it or how it interacts with other drugs. Pennsylvania urgently needs to regulate the sale of this drug to increase consumer safety.”
The bill now heads to the state Senate for consideration.

Rivera bill to lower electricity costs, increase reliability through grid-scale battery storage passes House
Rep. Nikki Rivera
October 5, 2026 | 4:05 PM
HARRISBURG, Oct. 5
– Legislation aimed at reducing electricity costs and increasing reliability for Pennsylvania households and small businesses by requiring electric utilities to set targets for and procure grid-stabilizing battery storage passed the House today, the bill’s prime sponsor, state Rep. Nikki Rivera, D-Lancaster, announced.
“Pennsylvania’s aging electricity grid is strained by increasingly violent weather and surging energy demand from cloud computing, artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies,” Rivera said. “My legislation offers a practical, proven solution that will help keep our lights on and our electric bills affordable.”
House Bill 2380
would require Pennsylvania’s largest electric utilities to install 3,500 megawatts of battery storage by 2035. The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission would assign each utility’s share of 3,500 megawatts based on the service load and annual peak demand of each electric company with more than 600,000 customers. The bill also includes competitive procurement requirements and regulatory oversight to help ensure projects deliver value for ratepayers.
Electricity costs are often driven by peak-hour demand, when electric utilities must rely on expensive “peaker” power plants that quickly ramp up to prevent grid failures. Battery storage systems store electricity when demand and prices are low and discharge it when demand is highest. They would lower costs by reducing congestion on the grid, limiting the need for expensive infrastructure upgrades, and cutting reliance on costly peak power purchases.
Rivera noted that the commonwealth’s energy usage grew nearly
3% in 2024
. She expressed concern that projected industrial demand growth over the next five years – particularly from data centers – would strain Pennsylvania’s energy grid.
Rivera pointed to the role that battery storage played in preventing blackouts during extreme summer heat in
California in 2021 and Texas in 2023
. She said that investment in battery storage is critical because the
PUC has warned
that the commonwealth’s grid could soon face widespread outages or even blackouts.
“Battery storage can help ensure that our grid remains reliable and resilient as demand grows and
extreme weather
puts greater pressure on the grid,” Rivera said. “Many of our residents in Central Pennsylvania, myself included, went without power for days this summer after the July 4 storm. A prolonged power outage during a blizzard would be devastating for Pennsylvania families and communities.”
Rivera pointed out that 13 states, including Maryland, New Jersey and New York, have adopted battery storage targets to lower costs, balance supply and demand and improve grid flexibility.
“It’s time for Pennsylvania to join its neighbors and modernize its power grid,” Rivera said. “We don’t have the time to waste.”
House Bill 2380 now moves to the Senate for consideration.

Pennsylvania benefits from growing Latino population
Lawmakers listen as experts detail obstacles, challenges
Rep. Nikki Rivera
September 22, 2026 | 12:43 PM
EASTON, Sept. 22
–
Pennsylvania’s growing Latino population is making important contributions to the commonwealth’s growing economy and workforce, while communities across the state continue working to address challenges facing Latino families and children.
The Pennsylvania Legislative Latino Caucus and House Majority Policy Committee today co-hosted a data-driven hearing on the state of the Latino community of Pennsylvania at the
Pennsylvania Latino Convention
in Easton.
“We are here to listen and learn what is working and what isn’t working, but more importantly, we are here to better understand what state lawmakers can do about it,” said Rep. Johanny Cepeda-Freytiz, who represents portions of Berks County and serves as the chairwoman of the Pennsylvania Legislative Latino Caucus. “The contributions of the Latino population to Pennsylvania are undeniable, but listening without action is just a conversation. We traveled here to learn more ideas and solutions, because our desire is to act.”
Experts detailed how Pennsylvania has welcomed Latinos into its workforce, a huge benefit in growing the state’s economy, but many times the children of Latino workers are struggling in the commonwealth’s education system.
“We heard it multiple times today: Pennsylvania has reaped incredible benefits from the Latino community, but we must do a better job serving our community and residents,” said Rep. Nikki Rivera, who represents portions of Lancaster County. “We are fighting for families like those we heard from today.”
Among the recommendations discussed during the hearing was the need to hire more bilingual teachers, bilingual teaching staff and bilingual school psychologists to better serve the state’s increasingly diverse schools.
“Pennsylvania’s Latino community is helping power our economy, strengthen our workforce and build stronger communities,” said Rep. Ryan Bizzarro, who serves as the House Majority Policy Committee chairman and represents portions of Erie County. “Our responsibility is to make sure every Latino family has a fair shot to succeed and the opportunity to thrive.”
Home ownership and income parity remain issues in the Latino community. Testifiers highlighted the growth of Pennsylvania’s youngest demographic, and its impressive number of entrepreneurs. However, the Latino population has the lowest median household income of any ethnic or racial group. Wages aren’t keeping pace with rising costs, squeezing workers and working families as communities are seeing an increase in food insecurity.
Consequently, the Latino population’s home ownership rate is below the state average, compounded by inequal access to credit for Latinos.

LANCASTER, Aug. 4
– State Rep. Nikki Rivera, D-Lancaster, announced today that Lancaster received a
Green Light-Go
grant of $494,466 to modernize traffic signals at two key intersections to improve safety and increase traffic flow for drivers, pedestrians and cyclists.
The funding will support upgrades to the traffic signal systems at North Duke Street and East Walnut Street and New Holland Avenue and Franklin Street to modernize aging infrastructure, increase signal reliability and accommodate increased traffic.

The Greenlight-Go Program is a competitive state grant program designed to improve the efficiency and operation of existing traffic signals in Pennsylvania and is administered by the state Transportation Department. Applicants are required to provide a 20% match. Funding may be used for traffic signal retiming; study and removal of unwarranted traffic-control signals; monitoring of traffic signal corridors; innovative technologies; installation, upgrade or maintenance of traffic signal communication systems; upgrade or installation of detection systems and controllers; modernization upgrades; implementation of intelligent transportation system applications; or to replace traditional or LED bulbs with new LED bulbs.

Smith-Wade-El, Rivera note passage of sentencing reform legislation
Rep. Nikki Rivera
July 24, 2026 | 11:39 AM
HARRISBURG, July 24
– State Reps. Ismail Smith-Wade-El and Nikki Rivera, both D-Lancaster, praised the actions of the PA House of Representatives in passing legislation that would end mandatory life-without-parole sentences in cases of second-degree felony murder in Pennsylvania.
In 2024, Derek Lee, a Black man serving life without parole for second-degree murder, challenged the constitutionality of his sentence before the Pennsylvania Supreme Court. He argued that since he did not kill or intend to kill anyone in a
2014 Pittsburgh robbery
, his sentence is disproportionate and cruel under both the Pennsylvania and U.S. constitutions.
This March, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court in Commonwealth v. Lee found that automatically imposing life without parole for all second-degree murder convictions violates the state constitution’s protections against cruel punishment because it does not consider individual responsibility or level of culpability.
Currently
only five states
— Pennsylvania, Iowa, Louisiana, Mississippi, and North Carolina — require mandatory life sentences without the possibility of parole for second-degree felony murder convictions.
The bill passed by the House (H.B. 1042) would require the Pennsylvania Commission on Sentencing to deliver guidelines to judges while still ensuring judges can examine the facts of each case. It also would allow certain incarcerated people who served more than 30 years of their sentence before the PA Supreme Court ruling to apply for parole and sets up requirements for victim notification, parole board recommendations, and judicial approval.
“Kudos to the advocates of this bill whose courage and tenacity has brought Pennsylvanians another step closer to a justice system that holds people accountable while honoring due process and humanity,” Smith-Wade-El said. “This bill is fundamentally about freedom: it liberates judges to exercise greater discernment and discretion in sentencing; provides incarcerated individuals with the hope of working towards rejoining their families and communities; and, at a societal level, frees us from costly and flawed sentencing practices rooted in fear to instead embrace rehabilitation and prevention."
“It is our job as legislators to ensure that everyone receives fair and constitutional treatment under our justice system and to continually improve that system so that everyone is treated justly,” Rivera said. “The House reconvened specifically to provide legislation that would give our justice system a  thoughtful and fair process to address those who are serving life sentences for second-degree murder.”
The representatives pointed out that while minorities make up only
27% of the state’s population
,
80% of people
serving life-without-parole sentences for felony murder are minorities
They contend that the bill, by replacing a mandatory sentence with individualized sentencing, could help reduce the disparate impact of Pennsylvania's felony murder sentencing laws while supporting judicial discretion and ensuring public safety.

Smith-Wade-El, Rivera urge Lancaster residents to get vaccinated against measles, stay informed with new dashboard
Rep. Nikki Rivera
July 15, 2026 | 2:22 PM
HARRISBURG, July 15
– As Lancaster County experiences the largest measles outbreak in Pennsylvania in 2026, state Reps. Ismail Smith-Wade-El and Nikki Rivera, both D-Lancaster, are encouraging residents to get vaccinated against the disease and to stay informed about outbreaks through the Pennsylvania Department of Health’s new measles online dashboard.
“We urge residents to protect themselves against the measles outbreak by getting vaccinated if they are unvaccinated and by staying informed about outbreaks using the Department of Health’s new online dashboard,” Smith-Wade-El and Rivera said in a joint statement. “We are grateful to the Department of Health for expanding public access to information and increasing transparency about measles cases in Pennsylvania.”
Since the beginning of the year, Pennsylvania has reported 105 cases of measles. More than half of those cases — 63 — have been reported in Lancaster County.
The new
online dashboard
provides up-to-date information on measles outbreaks across Pennsylvania, including case details by county, age and hospitalizations. The dashboard is updated every Monday, Wednesday and Friday afternoon with the latest available data.
The Department of Health currently provides
school vaccination data
at the county and state levels. In August, school-level vaccination information will be available online, giving families additional information to guide personal health and educational decisions.
“The one common thread among nearly all measles cases is that individuals are either unvaccinated or unable to confirm their vaccination status,” the representatives said. “For the sake of their families and their communities, we urge all eligible residents to get vaccinated against this preventable disease.”
The representatives also applauded the Department of Health’s response in Lancaster County to counteract the measles outbreak in 2026, including its pop-up measles vaccine clinics. Since cases were first identified in late April, the clinics have administered more than 600 vaccine doses in Lancaster County. By comparison, Department of Health staff administered 179 measles vaccinations in the county during all of 2025.
According to the Department of Health, measles had been
essentially eliminated
in the U.S. since 2000, thanks to the MMR vaccine, which is 97% effective.
Measles: What You Should Know
Measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus can remain in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person leaves the area.
Symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes (conjunctivitis), followed by a rash that begins on the face and spreads downward. Symptoms typically appear seven to 21 days after exposure. Measles can lead to serious complications, including hospitalization and death.
Anyone who believes they were exposed to measles and is experiencing symptoms should contact a health care provider before seeking in-person care or call the Department of Health’s toll-free hotline at 877-PA-HEALTH (877-724-3258).
More information on measles is available at
www.pa.gov/measles
.

House passes Rivera bill to increase transparency  and accountability in EITC program
Rep. Nikki Rivera
June 22, 2026 | 4:11 PM
HARRISBURG, June 22
– The Pennsylvania House today passed legislation (H.B. 2632) introduced by state Rep. Nikki Rivera that would increase accountability and transparency in the state’s Educational Improvement Tax Credit programs.
The bill would close reporting gaps and help ensure that program funds are reaching their intended recipients.
Rivera noted that EITC programs have grown to a $680 million public investment in nonpublic education for fiscal year 2025-26 -- more than four times the $150 million cap that existed a decade ago. Despite that growth, the Independent Fiscal Office has reported that significant data gaps make it difficult to fully evaluate the programs’ effectiveness.
“A $680 million annual scholarship tax program should be transparent and include detailed reporting,” Rivera said. “This bill would ensure that everyone can see how well EITC programs are working, whom they are helping, and whether students in private and parochial schools are receiving tuition relief.”
Rivera emphasized that the legislation would not reduce funding for the program.
“This bill would not cut one penny from the $680 million EITC program,” she said.
House Bill 2632 would require participating schools to provide basic information to the Department of Education, businesses redirecting tax dollars through the program to submit basic information to the Department of Revenue, and participating entities to undergo audits by the state Auditor General.
“By closing these reporting gaps, H.B. 2632 would provide the information needed to assess the effectiveness of EITC scholarships and evaluate their impact on students, schools, and taxpayers,” Rivera said.
The Educational Improvement Tax Credit program, established by Act 4 of 2001, allows businesses to reduce their state tax liability -- including the Corporate Net Income Tax and other taxes -- by contributing to approved scholarship and educational organizations.
“Our taxpayers deserve to know if their tax dollars are reaching the students they are intended to help and students deserve to receive the scholarships for which they qualify,” Rivera said. “H.B. 2632 provides the transparency needed to make that a reality.”
The legislation is now on its way to the Senate for consideration.

Rivera bill to lower electricity costs, increase reliability through grid-scale battery storage advances from committee
Rep. Nikki Rivera
June 18, 2026 | 10:52 AM
HARRISBURG, June 17
– Legislation aimed at reducing electricity costs and increasing reliability for Pennsylvania households and small businesses by requiring electric utilities to set targets for and procure grid-stabilizing battery storage cleared the Pennsylvania House Energy Committee today, the bill’s prime sponsor, state Rep. Nikki Rivera, D-Lancaster, announced.
“Increasing demand for energy for cloud computing, artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies is rapidly driving up electricity costs for Pennsylvanians,” Rivera said. “My legislation offers a practical, proven solution to help keep the lights on and electric bills affordable by requiring electric utilities to set targets for and invest in grid-stabilizing battery storage.”
House Bill 2380
would require Pennsylvania’s largest electric utilities to install 3,000 megawatts of battery storage by 2033. The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission would assign the shares of the 3,000 megawatts based on the service load and annual peak demand of each electric company with more than 600,000 customers.
Rivera’s plan would help lower costs by reducing congestion on the electric grid, limiting the need for expensive infrastructure upgrades and reducing reliance on costly peak-period power purchases. The bill also includes competitive procurement requirements and regulatory oversight to help ensure that projects deliver value for ratepayers.
“This bill is a smart investment in a stronger, more reliable and more affordable energy future for Pennsylvania families and businesses,” Rivera said.
Electricity costs are often driven by peak-hour demand, when electric utilities must rely on expensive “peaker” power plants that quickly ramp up to prevent grid failures. Battery storage systems store electricity when demand and prices are low and discharge it when demand is highest, helping stabilize the grid and reduce overall costs.
Battery storage would help lower costs by reducing congestion on the grid, limiting the need for expensive infrastructure upgrades, and cutting reliance on costly peak power purchases.
Rivera noted that the commonwealth’s energy usage grew nearly
3% in 2024
, and she expressed concern over how projected industrial demand growth projected over the next five years – particularly by data centers – would strain Pennsylvania’s energy grid.
She pointed out the role that battery storage played in preventing blackouts in extreme summer heats in
California in 2021 and Texas in 2023
. Rivera said that investment in battery storage is critical given
PUC has warned
that the commonwealth’s grid could soon face widespread outages, reduced reliability or even blackouts as early as this year.
“Battery storage can help ensure that our grid remains reliable and resilient as demand grows and
extreme weather
puts greater pressure on the grid,” Rivera said. “A prolonged power outage during a blizzard or other severe weather event would be devastating for Pennsylvania families and communities.”
Rivera pointed out that 13 states have already adopted battery storage targets to lower costs, balance supply and demand, and improve grid flexibility, including Maryland, New Jersey and New York.
“It’s time for Pennsylvania to join its neighbors and modernize its utility power system,” Rivera said.
House Bill 2380 is now with the full House for consideration.

House Energy Committee advances legislation to optimize electric grid, accelerate interconnection to meet rising energy demand
Rep. Nikki Rivera
June 17, 2026 | 3:56 PM
HARRISBURG, June 17
– Continuing its efforts to address the root causes of rising energy prices in Pennsylvania, the House Energy Committee voted favorably to advance key bills that leverage the state’s existing grid infrastructure and next-generation technologies to meet rising demand and improve grid reliability.
The bills are:
H.B. 2380
: Deploying Battery Storage to Meet Peak Demand.
H.B. 2595
: Reducing Interconnection Delays by Slashing Red Tape.
House Bill 2380, sponsored by Rep. Nikki Rivera, D-Lancaster, was approved by the committee by a 14-12 vote. The bill would establish targets for battery energy storage programs. By 2033 these programs would bring 3,000 megawatts of energy storage online by 2033, which is enough to power roughly 2.5 million homes.
Battery storage addresses one of Pennsylvania's most pressing energy challenges by storing high volumes of electricity when it’s plentiful and cheaper, and discharging it back to the grid when it’s needed most. At a recent public hearing on the bill, testifiers emphasized battery storage as a far more efficient method of stabilizing the grid during demand spikes than traditional “peaker plants.”
“Increasing demand for energy for cloud computing, artificial intelligence and more are making electricity unaffordable for Pennsylvanians,”
Rivera
said. “My legislation would help ensure electricity’s reliability and affordability by requiring electric utilities to set targets and procure grid-stabilizing battery storage.”
Thirteen states have already established targeted programs similar to those included in H.B. 2380, the most aggressive of which were set by California, New York and Texas.
The bill has earned the support of environmental organizations and industry stakeholders such as, Clean Air Council, Mid-Atlantic Renewable Energy Coalition, Solar Energy Industries Association and Advanced Energy United.
The committee unanimously approved H.B. 2595 sponsored by Rep. John Inglis, D-Allegheny. This bill would streamline the interconnection process by imposing strict deadlines on electric distribution company interconnection studies.
Interconnection delays create unpredictable project timelines for developers, ultimately increasing project costs and putting Pennsylvania at a competitive disadvantage. In neighboring states this process can be completed in as little as 60 days, but in Pennsylvania, interconnection processes often delay projects by 12 or more months.
“House Bill 2595’s bipartisan support shows the importance of adding more electricity to the grid as soon as possible. We cannot afford to have expanded energy generation and new opportunities delayed or abandoned. I’m grateful for my colleagues’ support and I look forward to seeing this move to a chamber vote soon,” said
Inglis
.
The bill is supported by key renewable energy associations such as PA Solar Center, Solar United Neighbors, Vote Solar and Solar Energy Industries Association. UGI Energy Services also expressed support for the bill.
“With costs rising, we know we need to meet energy demand, but we also know we have creative solutions, ways to get more out of our grid without expensive new infrastructure projects," said
Rep. Elizabeth Fiedler
, chair of the House Energy Committee. “By making it easier to get projects online and making smart use of the energy we produce during peak demand, Rep. Inglis and Rep. Rivera’s bills will strengthen our grid and better prepare our energy sector for a changing world.”
The committee also voted favorably on Rep. Joe Ciresi’s
H.B. 2359
, which would adjust the Computer Data Center Sales and Use Tax Exemption Program, adding community protection eligibility requirements.
All three bills now move to the full House chamber for further consideration.

Rivera’s bill to close EITC reporting gaps introduced
Rep. Nikki Rivera
June 12, 2026 | 4:54 PM
HARRISBURG, June 12
– State Rep. Nikki Rivera, D-Lancaster, today introduced H.B. 2632 which would improve transparency in Educational Improvement Tax Credit programs by closing reporting gaps to ensure that funds are directed to their intended recipients.
Rivera said EITC programs have grown into a $680 million public investment in nonpublic education in fiscal year 2025-26, more than four times the $150 million cap in place a decade ago. However, the Independent Fiscal Office has found that critical data gaps make it impossible to fully evaluate the program's effectiveness.
“While EITC funding has quadrupled over the last decade, key reporting gaps have left lawmakers and taxpayers unable to assess whether public funds have reached the students and schools they were intended to aid,” Rivera said. “That should concern everyone.
“My legislation would close these reporting gaps and ensure greater accountability so we know that these scholarships have reached the intended students.”
House Bill 2632 would:
Reallocate credits in 2026-27 to better align with program demand.
Create a new program beginning in 2027-28. The new program would:
Increase oversight of scholarship granting organizations.
Target resources to students living in the attendance area of a low-achieving public school or attending a nonpublic school in a low-income ZIP code.
Increase transparency on how scholarship dollars are used, including requiring reporting by income level and amount of remaining tuition charged to the student.
Expand funding opportunities to include childcare costs.
“These reporting gaps leave lawmakers without the information necessary to determine whether the EITC program is fulfilling its goals and reaching the students in need,” Rivera said. “By closing those gaps, H.B. 2632 would provide the transparency needed to assess whether resources have been distributed effectively and evaluate these scholarships’ impact on students, schools and taxpayers.”
The Educational Improvement Tax Credit, established by Act 4 of 2001, potentially allows businesses to significantly reduce their state tax liability (e.g., Corporate Net Income Tax, Capital Stock Franchise Tax, Bank and Trust Company Shares Tax, Title Insurance Companies Shares Tax, Insurance Premiums Tax and/or Mutual Thrift Institution Tax) by contributing/donating (cash, personal property or services) to a nonprofit educational improvement or nonprofit scholarship organization.

Rep. Nikki Rivera
June 12, 2026 | 9:38 AM
LANCASTER, June 11 – Building on the success of her May event promoting Red Rose Authority’s services, state Rep. Nikki Rivera, D-Lancaster, will lead a second “Bus it to Market” trip on Saturday, June 27, to Central Market in Lancaster to raise awareness of the region’s affordable bus transportation system.
“Residents on last month’s ‘Bus it to Market’ trip told me how much they enjoyed the ease and affordability of RRTA’s bus ride to Central Market,” Rivera said. “I’m leading a second ride so that more of our residents can experience for themselves how central Lancaster City’s eclectic mix of one-of-a-kind shops and creative restaurants is just a short RRTA bus ride away. And knowledge of how to use our public transportation can lead to new job opportunities.”
Rivera said that she hopes her Bus It to Market excursions will show residents that RRTA buses are a fast, reliable, and inexpensive way to get to Lancaster and other places in the region.
According to Rivera, Lancaster has unhealthy levels of air pollution. She cited the
American Lung Association’s 2025 “State of the Air”
report, which listed the Lancaster metro area as rejoining the worst 25 cities in the U.S., at 22nd most polluted in the nation and second worst in the Mid-Atlantic for daily particle pollution. The Lancaster area’s year-round pollution went from bad to worse, from 57th to 45th worst in the nation for year-round pollution and dropped from a B grade for ozone in last year’s report to a C grade.
“Air pollution is damaging our health, especially impacting people with respiratory problems and seniors,” Rivera said. “Regularly taking the bus can help reduce air pollution in our area. Congested roadways, limited street parking, the high cost of parking -- who needs any of it when you can take the bus?”
Trip attendees will join Rivera at 9:15 a.m. on June 27 at the Stubby's Bar and Grille parking lot, 701 Olde Hickory Road at Oregon Pike, in Manheim Township. Together, they will walk across the street to Valleybrook Estates to the bus shelter.
If adult attendees do not have an RRTA Go Mobile app or a reusable Go Mobile Smart Card, they will need exact change for the ride to and from Lancaster.
Fare costs:
• Adult fare: $1.80
• K–12 student fare: $1.00
• Half Fare Program for persons with disabilities: $0.90
Adults 65 or older can ride for free if they have a senior ID card. If they do not have one, they can apply here:
Senior Citizens Free Ride Program – Red Rose Transit Authority
. For people with disabilities, the fare is $0.90.
On the bus ride, an RRTA representative will provide valuable information about the bus transportation system. On arrival, the group will walk to Central Market, spend some time enjoying the Lancaster downtown shops and cafés, and return to the ChargePoint Charging Station parking lot in Lancaster by 1:20 p.m.
Residents interested in joining “Bus It to Market” should RSVP by emailing
reprivera@pahouse.net
by June 26. In the email, those interested should note how many people will be joining them for the trip.

Rep. Nikki Rivera
October 19, 2026 | 2:27 PM
HARRISBURG, Oct 19
– In early September, the PUC released a dire
report
warning about Pennsylvania’s energy future: because of the skyrocketing demand brought on by AI data centers, blackouts and other grid failures could be six times worse than PJM’s planning standard by 2030.
House Democrats and the House Energy Committee today announced a comprehensive, three-pronged approach to addressing and reversing this crisis: generation, efficiency and
demand response.
The bills in the package are:
H.B. 2347: PEDA Modernization (Fiedler)
H.B. 2651: Siting New Energy Projects (Steele)
H.B. 505: Modernizing Energy Efficiency in the Commonwealth (Donahue)
H.B. 660: Energy Efficient Appliances (O’Mara)
H.B. 2264: Establishing a Virtual Power Plant (VPP) Program (Davidson)
H.B. 2380: Reducing utility bills by utilizing grid-scale battery storage (Rivera)
“The House Energy Committee has been sounding the alarm on this crisis since day one. We’ve put forward bills that would increase generation, stabilize and modernize our grid, and help us meet demand at those vulnerable, peak moments when power outages are most likely to occur,” said
Rep. Elizabeth Fiedler,
committee
chair
.
“My bill to modernize PEDA as a financing authority would unlock new energy supply, encourage innovation and put people to work across Pennsylvania.”

Rivera legislation protecting children from online victimization and hazing heads to the governor’s desk: Bill tightens mandated reporter obligations in the age of AI
Rep. Nikki Rivera
October 21, 2026 | 5:08 PM
HARRISBURG, Oct. 21
– Bipartisan legislation to better protect Pennsylvania’s children from sexually explicit Artificial Intelligence-generated deepfakes and hazing is headed to the governor’s desk, according to the bill’s sponsor, state Rep. Nikki Rivera, D-Lancaster.
House Bill 2474 expands Pennsylvania’s Child Protective Services Law to cover more forms of harm to children, including harm caused by other children. This bill adds the unlawful distribution of intimate images, sexually abusive materials, hazing and aggravated hazing to the offenses that must be reported.
The bill requires all mandated reporters, not just school personnel, to quickly report to Childline, the statewide toll-free number for reporting child abuse and well-being concern, whenever they have reasonable cause to believe child sex abuse material exists or that hazing or aggravated hazing has occurred. Materials include AI-generated material or material created or shared by a minor.
The Department of Human Services will then forward each report to law enforcement so authorities can act quickly. The bill will ensure that authorities can immediately act to protect children and prevent further harm. The law will take effect 90 days after enactment
“The rise of AI has made our children more vulnerable to exploitation and bullying so we’re acting decisively to protect our children from this evolving threat--AI-generated deepfakes--by passing this bill,” Rivera said. “This legislation is a commonsense, urgently necessary step that clarifies mandated reporters’ responsibilities, supports investigators’ efforts to track down perpetrators and reinforces our commitment to protecting the safety and dignity of every student in Pennsylvania.”
Rivera said two incidents in Lancaster and Bucks counties -- both involving students using artificial intelligence to spread sexually explicit images of their classmates -- prompted her and co-sponsor state Rep. Kristin Marcell, R-Bucks, to introduce the bill.
In 2023, two students at a Lancaster County private school used AI to create sexually explicit deepfake images of 48 schoolmates and 12 other students. In 2025, two Bucks County public middle school students created sexually explicit deepfake images depicting 12 fellow female students, which were then shared among other students in the district. In both cases, the dissemination of the pornographic AI images went unreported to law enforcement, resulting in more child sexual abuse material being shared and more victims being targeted.
“House Bill 2474 makes it crystal clear that mandated reporters must immediately report to authorities when a child is creating child sexual abuse material or hazing another student,” Rivera said. “By taking the guesswork out of the equation, this bill goes a long way toward ensuring that all adults responsible for children report crimes against minors in a timely, efficient manner to prevent any further abuse. This necessary reform of our mandated reporting requirements will strengthen our system of care and make our children safer.”

Rep. Nikki Rivera
October 27, 2026 | 4:12 PM
HARRISBURG, Oct. 27
– State Rep. Nikki Rivera, D-Lancaster, praised the Shapiro Administration for investing more than $441,000 in community revitalization projects locally.
The state Neighborhood Assistance Program provides tax credits to businesses that contribute to nonprofit organizations’ efforts to revitalize communities. Through the NAP, businesses can receive tax credits of up to 95% for contributions they make to a qualifying community project. Projects must fall into one of the following categories: affordable housing programs, community services, crime prevention, education, job training, or neighborhood assistance.
“Our residents are struggling to find affordable housing,” Rivera said. “These tax credits will help increase housing stock in our area as well as strengthen outreach for the unhoused, connecting them to housing, jobs, health care, and other basic needs.”
The NAP has five main components: the Neighborhood Assistance Program, Special Program Priorities, the Neighborhood Partnership Program, the Charitable Food Program, and the Enterprise Zone Program.
The following organizations received tax credits:
Special Priorities Program
$162,000       Lancaster Area Habitat for Humanity to construct eight affordable units on Wheatland Avenue in Lancaster.
$31,050         Lancaster County Food Hub to expand outreach services for neighbors experiencing homelessness including connections to housing, jobs, healthcare, and basic needs.
$209,925       YWCA of Lancaster to complete pre-construction design stage to renovate 18 affordable units, 6 efficiencies, and modernize shared spaces.
$38,250         United Way of Lancaster to expand 2 1-1 Housing & Homelessness Navigation to help individuals experiencing homelessness connect to community resources, housing support services, and shelters
